subChunks.title: Functional Interfaces & Lambda Syntax
subChunks.hookHtml: Imagine if you could hand a behaviour to a method — not just data, but a tiny piece of logic wrapped up and passed like a scroll. That is exactly what lambdas give you: concise, powerful expressions of behaviour that treat code as a first-class citizen.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is a Functional Interface?

A functional interface is any interface that declares exactly one abstract method. That single contract is what makes it compatible with a lambda expression. The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended — it causes the compiler to enforce the one-abstract-method rule.

@FunctionalInterface
interface Greet {
    String greetings(String name); // only one abstract method
}

// Using a lambda instead of an anonymous class:
Greet g = name -> "Hello, " + name + "!";
System.out.println(g.greetings("Eldrin")); // Hello, Eldrin!

The Four Built-In Functional Interfaces

Java's java.util.function package ships four core interfaces that cover almost every situation:

// Predicate  — takes T, returns boolean
Predicate<Integer> isAdult = age -> age >= 18;
System.out.println(isAdult.test(21)); // true
System.out.println(isAdult.test(14)); // false

// Function  — takes T, returns R
Function<String, Integer> strLen = s -> s.length();
System.out.println(strLen.apply("Fireball")); // 8

// Consumer  — takes T, returns nothing (side-effect only)
Consumer<String> printer = s -> System.out.println(">> " + s);
printer.accept("Casting Frost Nova"); // >> Casting Frost Nova

// Supplier  — takes nothing, returns T
Supplier<String> randomSpell = () -> "Blizzard";
System.out.println(randomSpell.get()); // Blizzard

Lambda Syntax and Capturing Variables

Lambda syntax is flexible. Parentheses around the parameter are optional when there is exactly one parameter; curly braces and return are optional when the body is a single expression. Lambdas may capture variables from their enclosing scope only if those variables are effectively final (never reassigned after their first assignment).

// Various valid lambda forms:
Predicate<String> isEmpty = s -> s.isEmpty();      // one param, no parens needed
Function<Integer,Integer> square = (n) -> n * n;    // one param with parens
BiFunction<Integer,Integer,Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b; // two params

// Multi-statement body needs braces + return:
Function<String, String> shout = s -> {
    String upper = s.toUpperCase();
    return upper + "!!!";
};

// Capturing an effectively-final variable:
String prefix = "Spell: ";                   // effectively final
Consumer<String> tag = s -> System.out.println(prefix + s);
tag.accept("Arcane Bolt"); // Spell: Arcane Bolt

Method References (::)

When a lambda does nothing but forward its argument(s) to an existing method, a method reference is cleaner.

// Static method reference
Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
System.out.println(parse.apply("42")); // 42

// Instance method reference on a particular object
String greeting = "Arcane Academy";
Supplier<Integer> len = greeting::length;
System.out.println(len.get()); // 14

// Instance method reference on an arbitrary instance of a type
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
System.out.println(upper.apply("fireball")); // FIREBALL

// Constructor reference
Supplier<StringBuilder> sbFactory = StringBuilder::new;
StringBuilder sb = sbFactory.get();

storyBeats.text: Deep in the Arcane Academy's Lambdarium, rows of crystalline scrolls glow with distilled logic — each one a tiny spell of behaviour, waiting to be passed to whatever ritual requires it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Welcome, apprentice. Until now you have passed *data* to your methods — integers, strings, objects. But true mastery begins when you pass *behaviour* itself. That is the gift of functional interfaces and lambdas.

storyBeats.speaker: Functional Interface
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice how the lambda replaces an entire anonymous class. Java's standard library provides four essential functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier. Learn these four and you can express almost any transformation.

storyBeats.speaker: The Four Core Interfaces
storyBeats.text:
Predicate<Integer> isPositive = n -> n > 0;     // test
Function<String,String> shout = s -> s + "!";    // transform
Consumer<String> log = s -> System.out.println(s); // consume
Supplier<Integer> roll = () -> 42;                // produce

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when your lambda merely calls a single existing method, use a method reference — the :: notation. It reads like a citation in a tome: 'use *this* method from *this* class.'
The apprentice studies the glowing scrolls, realising that lambdas are not just syntax sugar — they are a new way of thinking about code: behaviour as data, logic as values.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Cast three functional spells in a single Main class:

  1. Create a Predicate<Integer> named isGreaterThanTen that returns true if the number is greater than 10. Test it on 15 and 5, printing each result.
  2. Create a Function<String, String> named shout that converts a string to uppercase and appends "!". Apply it to "arcane" and print the result.
  3. Create a Consumer<String> named castingAnnouncer that prints "Casting: " followed by the string. Use it with "Fireball".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier in your own words. Include: why would you choose one over another, and what does 'effectively final' mean when capturing a variable in a lambda?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank slate, write a Main class that does all three tasks without any starter code:

  1. A Predicate<Integer> testing whether a number is greater than 10 — test on 15 and 5.
  2. A Function<String,String> that uppercases and appends ! — apply to "arcane".
  3. A Consumer<String> that prints "Casting: " + the value — use with "Fireball".

rabbitHoleTerms.description: An anonymous function expressed inline, using the -> arrow syntax, that can be treated as an object implementing a functional interface.
An interface with exactly one abstract method, enabling lambda expressions and method references to be used wherever it is expected.
A functional interface whose test(T t) method returns a boolean — used for filtering and condition checks.
A functional interface whose accept(T t) method returns void — used for operations with side effects such as printing.
A functional interface whose apply(T t) method returns R — used for transforming a value from one type to another.
A functional interface whose get() method takes no arguments and returns T — used for lazy value production.
A shorthand for a lambda that simply calls an existing method, using the :: operator (e.g. String::toUpperCase).
A local variable that is never reassigned after its initial assignment; lambdas can capture effectively-final variables from their enclosing scope.

questions.questionHtml: Which built-in functional interface takes a value and returns void?
questions.explanationHtml: Consumer<T> is designed for operations that consume a value and produce no result — its single abstract method is void accept(T t). This makes it ideal for side-effectful actions like printing or logging. Predicate returns a boolean, Function returns a value of type R, and Supplier produces a value without consuming one.

f.apply("magic") calls toUpperCase() on "magic" producing "MAGIC", then appends "!" to get "MAGIC!". p.test("magic") checks whether the length (5) is greater than 5 — it is not, so it prints false. Note the boundary: greater-than (strict), not greater-than-or-equal.

questions.questionHtml: This code fails to compile. What is the bug?
questions.correctAnswer: The variable 'prefix' is reassigned after its first assignment, so it is not effectively final and cannot be captured by the lambda.
questions.explanationHtml: Java lambdas can only capture local variables from the enclosing scope if they are effectively final — meaning they are never reassigned after their first assignment. Here, prefix is assigned twice ("Result: " then "Answer: "), so the compiler rejects the lambda. The fix is to remove the second assignment, or copy the value into a new final variable: String p = prefix; and capture p instead.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is the correct method reference equivalent of s -> s.toUpperCase()?
questions.explanationHtml: String::toUpperCase is an instance method reference on an arbitrary instance of String. When used as a Function<String,String>, Java understands it as: for a given String s, call s.toUpperCase(). String::new is a constructor reference, System.out::println is a bound instance method reference on a specific object (System.out), and String::valueOf is a static method reference.

subChunks.title: Comparator and Sorting with Lambdas
subChunks.hookHtml: A Comparator is the arcane sorting rune of Java. With lambdas, writing custom sort orders becomes elegant — no more verbose anonymous classes, just clear, composable comparison logic that sorts your collections exactly the way you need.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Comparator Basics

The Comparator<T> interface has one abstract method: int compare(T o1, T o2). It returns negative if o1 should come first, zero if equal, positive if o2 should come first. Before Java 8, you'd write an anonymous class; now a lambda does the same job in one line.

List<String> spells = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Blizzard", "Fireball", "Arc"));

// Anonymous class style (old)
spells.sort(new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.compareTo(b); }
});

// Lambda style (modern)
spells.sort((a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));

// Method reference style (most concise)
spells.sort(String::compareTo);

Comparator.comparing() and Chaining

Comparator.comparing() accepts a key-extractor function and builds a Comparator from it. You can chain multiple sort criteria with thenComparing(), and reverse any Comparator with reversed().

// Sort by string length
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

// Sort by length, then alphabetically for ties
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
            .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));

// Reverse alphabetical
spells.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder().reversed());

// Using Comparator.comparing with a lambda key extractor:
spells.sort(Comparator.comparing(s -> s.substring(0, 1))); // first letter

Sorting Arrays and Custom Objects

Arrays.sort() also accepts a Comparator. When sorting custom objects, extract a field with a getter and pass it to Comparator.comparing().

String[] arr = {"Zap", "Arc", "Blizzard"};
Arrays.sort(arr); // natural order (alphabetical)
Arrays.sort(arr, Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)); // by length

// Custom object example:
record Spell(String name, int damage) {}
List<Spell> spellList = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
    new Spell("Fireball", 80),
    new Spell("Frost", 60),
    new Spell("Thunder", 90)
));
spellList.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Spell::damage).reversed());
// Now: Thunder(90), Fireball(80), Frost(60)

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Grand Sorting Hall is where apprentices learn to arrange their knowledge — spells catalogued by name, power, rarity. Without a Comparator, chaos reigns.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every collection must eventually be ordered. The Comparator is your sorting rune. In the old days, you'd write entire anonymous classes for a single comparison. Lambdas reduce that ceremony to a single expressive line.

storyBeats.speaker: Lambda Sort
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But the real power comes from Comparator.comparing() — it lets you extract a sort key cleanly. Chain thenComparing() for secondary sorts, and reversed() to flip the order entirely.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Remember: Comparator is a functional interface. Any lambda with the signature (T, T) -> int is a valid Comparator. The standard library methods like comparing() are just convenient factory methods that build Comparators for you.
The apprentice sorts the Academy's spell registry in seconds — alphabetically, by power, by rarity — all with crisp, readable lambda expressions.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:

  1. Create ArrayList<String> spells = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Blizzard","Fireball","Arc","Zap","Earthquake")). Sort alphabetically and print each spell on its own line.
  2. Sort the same list by length ascending (shortest first) and print each spell on its own line.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain how Comparator.comparing() works in your own words. What does it mean to chain comparators with thenComparing(), and how is that different from writing a single complex lambda?

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A functional interface for defining custom ordering; its compare(T o1, T o2) method returns negative, zero, or positive to indicate order.
A static factory method that creates a Comparator from a key-extraction function, making it easy to sort by a specific field.
A Comparator method that adds a secondary sort criterion, applied when the primary comparator considers two elements equal.
A Comparator method that returns a new Comparator with the ordering flipped.
The default sort order for Comparable objects (e.g. alphabetical for Strings, numeric for Integers), accessible via Comparator.naturalOrder().
An interface a class implements to define its natural ordering via the compareTo() method; distinct from Comparator which is an external ordering strategy.

options: A new List in reverse order
A Comparator with the ordering flipped
A Comparator that sorts by length descending
questions.correctAnswer: A Comparator with the ordering flipped
questions.explanationHtml: reversed() is a default method on the Comparator interface that returns a new Comparator wrapping the original, with the comparison result negated. The original Comparator is unchanged (Comparators are typically immutable). It does not sort by any particular field — it simply mirrors whatever ordering the original Comparator defined.

Sorting by length ascending: Ox (2) < Cat (3) = Dog (3) < Elephant (8). So words.get(0) is "Ox" and words.get(words.size()-1) is "Elephant". The tie between Cat and Dog is resolved by the sort algorithm's stability (their relative order is preserved from the original list).

questions.questionHtml: This code throws an UnsupportedOperationException at runtime. Why?
questions.correctAnswer: List.of() returns an unmodifiable list, so calling sort() on it throws UnsupportedOperationException. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>() to get a mutable copy.
questions.explanationHtml: List.of() creates an immutable list. Calling any mutating method on it — including sort(), add(), or remove() — throws UnsupportedOperationException. The fix is to wrap the list: new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)), which creates a mutable ArrayList initialised with those elements. This is a very common pitfall when using the factory methods introduced in Java 9.

questions.questionHtml: You want to sort a list of spells first by damage descending, then alphabetically for ties. Which is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: The key insight is that reversed() reverses the entire comparator chain built so far, not just the next step. By calling .reversed() right after comparingInt(Spell::damage) (and before thenComparing), only the damage ordering is reversed. Then thenComparing(Spell::name) adds alphabetical as a secondary criterion in its natural (ascending) order. Option C reverses the whole final comparator — flipping both damage AND name order, which is wrong. Option D is not a valid API call.
